items.followUp: Describe the role of the small intestine in human digestion.

rubric.why: This point identifies the stomach’s role in holding food before digestion continues.
rubric.how: State that food is stored or held temporarily in the stomach.

rubric.why: This point describes the stomach’s mechanical action and its mixing of food with gastric juice.
rubric.description: Muscular contractions churn and mix food with gastric juice.
rubric.how: Mention churning or mixing food with gastric juice.

rubric.why: This point identifies the main gastric juice components and their roles in protein digestion.
rubric.description: Hydrochloric acid provides an acidic medium, and pepsin begins protein digestion.
rubric.how: Name the acidic medium and pepsin’s action on proteins.

rubric.why: This point gives an additional function or the fate of partly digested food.
rubric.description: Mucus protects the stomach lining; partly digested food called chyme passes to the small intestine.
rubric.how: State either that mucus protects the stomach lining or that chyme passes into the small intestine.

modelAnswer: The stomach is a muscular sac that temporarily stores food.
Its muscular walls churn and mix food with gastric juice.
Hydrochloric acid in the gastric juice provides an acidic medium, while pepsin begins the digestion of proteins.
Mucus protects the stomach lining, and the partly digested food, called chyme, passes into the small intestine.

items.followUp: Define population and state its two types.

rubric.why: This point states the defining features of a community.
rubric.description: A community consists of populations of different species living in the same area or habitat.
rubric.how: Include different species or their populations and a shared area or habitat.

rubric.why: This point names both types of community.
rubric.description: The two types are major communities and minor communities.
rubric.how: Name both major and minor communities.

modelAnswer: A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area or habitat.
Communities are of two types: major communities and minor communities.

items.followUp: Give one example each of a quantitative and a qualitative observation.

rubric.why: This point identifies that quantitative observations are expressed numerically or as measurements.
rubric.description: Quantitative observations are expressed as numbers or measurements.
rubric.how: State that quantitative observations are numerical or measurable.

rubric.why: This point gives a valid advantage of quantitative observations over qualitative ones.
rubric.description: They are generally more objective and precise, and easier to compare and analyze.
rubric.how: Give at least one valid reason they are better, such as being more objective, precise, or easier to compare or analyze.

modelAnswer: Quantitative observations are expressed as numbers or measurements.
They are generally more objective and precise than qualitative observations, and are easier to compare and analyze.

items.followUp: What is osmosis, and does it require cellular energy?

rubric.why: This point describes passive transport as movement down a concentration gradient without energy.
rubric.description: Passive transport moves substances from higher to lower concentration without using cellular energy.
rubric.how: State that passive transport moves down the concentration gradient or from high to low concentration, without energy.

rubric.why: This point contrasts active transport with passive transport by stating its direction and energy requirement.
rubric.description: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient and requires energy, usually ATP.
rubric.how: State that active transport moves against the gradient and requires energy or ATP.

modelAnswer: Passive transport moves substances down their concentration gradient, from higher to lower concentration, without using cellular energy.
Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration, and requires energy, usually ATP.
